372.title: The heart's wish
372.hook: pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa: may my heart's longing be fulfilled, my mind rest at Your feet (Chaupai)
372.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these lines in Chaupai Sahib morning and evening, and they are often quoted in Sikh teaching as a prayer for the longing to stay near God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rachhaa, protection, and your line, keep me by the hand. Now the second line, about the heart.

Ask a child what they wish for and you'll get a list: a puppy, a bike, to stay up late. Ask a teenager and the list changes. Ask someone in their forties and it changes again. Ask someone at the end of a long life and the list usually gets very short, often one or two things, almost never things you can buy. Underneath all the lists is a deepest wish, the one that rarely gets said out loud. Chaupai's second line asks for exactly that wish to be fulfilled.
screen: `A CHILD'S LIST OF WISHES.` → `THE LIST GETS SHORTER WITH AGE.` → `THE DEEPEST WISH, UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: The line is pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa. Pooran: full, complete, fulfilled. Chit: the mind, the heart, your inner awareness. Ichhaa: wish, longing. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Sikh teaching is often wary of wanting. The Guru Granth Sahib warns again and again about trishna, the thirst that never stops, the craving that eats a life. So how can Chaupai ask God to fulfill a wish? Because of the very next line. In paraphrase: may my mind remain at your feet. The two lines come as a pair. The wish isn't the puppy or the bike. It's the deepest one, to stay close to the One. In Sikh imagery, the feet are the place of humility and nearness, where you sit when you've stopped trying to be in charge. Later in the same prayer, the wish comes back. In paraphrase: may my hope be fulfilled, and may my thirst for your praise remain. A prayer that asks for one thirst never to be quenched. Other cravings, the tradition says, leave a person emptier. This one, as Sikhs read it, is the opposite: a thirst that fills while it stays a thirst. So the line isn't a blank check. It's a question with an answer folded inside: what does your heart want, underneath the list? Chaupai's answer is to stay at the feet, and to keep wanting that.

segments.voice: Let the surface wishes come first, the things you want this week, this year, and let them pass like cars going by. Then ask quietly what you want most underneath all of them, to be at peace, to be close to someone, to be close to God, to be good, and give it time. When something feels true, name it in a few words; if you pray, offer it with Waheguru.
Ichhaa, wish or longing. Pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa: may my heart's longing be fulfilled, paired with the line that names it, to stay at the Lord's feet.
Your line: stay at the feet. One thirst worth keeping. Day three hundred seventy-two, done.

373.title: The enemies within and without
373.hook: the prayer asks for enemies to be ended; many read them also as the five thieves inside
373.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these lines of Chaupai Sahib daily, understanding the enemies both as outward threats and as the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ichhaa, the heart's wish, and your line, stay at the feet. Today the prayer turns to something harder.

Anandpur, in the last years of the sixteen hundreds. The Tenth Guru's town sits in the hills, and the hills are full of trouble. Neighboring kings resent him. Imperial armies will later come. There will be sieges, hunger, a night when the town has to be left behind. These aren't metaphors; they're men with weapons, and they're coming. In this world, the Guru writes a prayer that asks, plainly, for enemies to be ended. It's a line people stumble over when they first read Chaupai.
screen: `ANANDPUR, IN THE HILLS.` → `REAL ARMIES, REAL SIEGES.` → `A PRAYER ABOUT ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: The lines come right after ichhaa. In paraphrase: destroy all my enemies; save me with your own hand. May my family live in peace, and all my servants and Sikhs. A little later: protect me with your own hand, and end all my foes this very day. The word for enemy here is dusht, the wicked, the one who means harm. Sikhs read these lines in two ways, and they don't have to choose. The first is the plain one. The Guru and his community faced real violence, and this is a leader asking God to protect his people from those who would kill them. The tradition doesn't apologize for that; asking for protection from harm isn't hatred. The second goes inside. The Guru Granth Sahib speaks again and again of five thieves in every person: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. They live inside the body, the scripture says, and plunder its treasure. Many Sikhs, saying Chaupai every day, hear the enemies as those five too. The dusht that harms you most on an ordinary Tuesday probably isn't an army. It's your anger at the driver who cut you off, the greed that keeps you scrolling, the ego that can't say sorry. Notice where the prayer puts the fight. It doesn't say, let me destroy them. It says, you destroy them, and save me with your hand. The battle, inner or outer, is handed over. In the prayer's picture, the enemy within doesn't go because it's hated. It goes when the one praying is held by something stronger.

segments.voice: Think of the five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego, and without listing all your faults, notice which one has been busiest in you lately, and name it in one word. Then, instead of fighting it, picture handing it over, the way the prayer does. If you pray, say Waheguru as you do; if not, just let your grip on it loosen a little.

374.title: Keep my Sikhs
374.hook: sevak sikh hamaare taareeh: carry my servants and Sikhs across (Chaupai)
374.tomorrow: The one who spreads and gathers
374.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within Chaupai Sahib daily; Sikh prayer, especially the Ardas, typically widens from oneself to family, community and finally the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dusht, the wicked, and your line, end the enemy within. Today the prayer turns outward again, to people.

A wide river in flood, the kind people in Punjab knew well, brown and fast and far too deep to wade. On this bank, everyone you love. On the far bank, safety. There's one boat, and one person who knows how to steer it. You don't ask for yourself first. You ask for them: take my mother, take my friend, take the kids. Get them across. That picture of a river and a crossing runs all through Sikh scripture, and in Chaupai the Guru uses it to pray for his people.
screen: `A RIVER IN FLOOD.` → `ONE BOAT, ONE PERSON TO STEER.` → `GET THEM ACROSS.`

segments.voice: The line is sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi. Sevak: servants, those who serve. Sikh: learners, disciples. Hamaare: mine. Taareeahi: carry them across. The verb is from taarna, to ferry over, to bring someone safely to the other shore. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the world is often pictured as a vast, terrifying ocean, and the Guru, or the Name, as the boat that carries people over it. So the Tenth Guru is doing something tender here: a Guru praying for his disciples, asking God to carry them across. Look how the prayer's circle has widened. First, protect me. Then, may my family live in peace. Then, all my servants and Sikhs. Sikh prayer often widens like that. The Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, names the Gurus, the martyrs, the community, and ends by asking for the good of all, everyone, without exception. You met that on day three hundred thirty. One more thing. This prayer is said by the community itself, every morning and evening. So a Sikh reciting it is saying a prayer the Guru prayed for them. Carry them across lands differently when you know you're one of the them.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one friend in a hard river right now, illness, grief, a bad job, a lonely stretch; see their face and say their name quietly. If you pray, hold that name in Waheguru or say the line, carry them across; if not, hold them in your attention and wish them safely to the other bank. Then, if it feels right, let the circle widen: one more name, then everyone in a river like theirs.

Your line: carry them across. The circle keeps widening, from me to everyone. Day three hundred seventy-four.

375.title: The one who spreads and gathers
375.hook: the Creator spreads creation out and draws it back into Himself (Chaupai)
375.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these verses of Chaupai Sahib daily, and Sikh teaching describes creation as flowing out from the One and merging back into the One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sevak sikh, and your line, carry them across. Today Chaupai widens all the way, to the whole of creation.

A jellyfish opens, wide and slow, like an umbrella, then closes, pulling itself in, and in that closing it moves forward. Open, close. Spread out, gather in. Your own chest is doing the same thing right now. Out, in. Lungs, tides, seasons, a beating heart: so much of the living world runs on that one rhythm. Chaupai takes it and applies it to the biggest thing there is.
screen: `A JELLYFISH OPENS AND CLOSES.` → `OUT, IN. LUNGS, TIDES, A HEART.` → `THE RHYTHM AT THE BIGGEST SCALE.`

segments.voice: In the middle of Chaupai, the prayer stops asking and simply looks at God. In paraphrase: when the Creator spreads creation out, beings take bodies beyond number. And when, at any time, you draw it back in, all bodies merge back into you. The two old words are udkarakh, spreading out, and aakarakh, drawing in. In this picture, the universe is the Creator's long breath. Breathe out, and there are galaxies, rivers, people, ants. Breathe in, and everything returns to the One it came from. It echoes the Japji, where Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that with a single word the Creator made the vast expanse, and from it a million rivers flowed. Creation in Sikh thought isn't a machine built once and left to run. It flows out of the One, and it's held in the One the whole time. Why is this in a prayer for protection? Because it changes what being kept means. If everything came out of the One and returns to the One, nothing that happens to you happens outside God. Even the drawing in, the ending of things, which frightens us most, is described as merging, not vanishing. That doesn't make loss painless; Sikhs grieve like everyone else. But it puts loss inside something larger and kinder. The hand that spread you out is the hand that gathers you in, and your own breath is a small copy of that.

segments.voice: Start with the out-breath, long and slow, as if spreading something into the room; pause; then let the in-breath come by itself, gathering back. Don't force it: let it be the rhythm your body already knows. If you pray, let Waheguru ride on the breath, wahe on the way out, guru on the way in; if not, just watch the two halves of each breath.
Kartaar, the Creator. Udkarakh and aakarakh: spreading creation out into countless bodies, and drawing it all back to merge in the One.
Your line: spread and gathered. The same hand does both, out and in. Until tomorrow.

376.title: Knower of every heart
376.hook: ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat: He knows every heart and recognizes the pain of good and bad alike (Chaupai)
376.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within Chaupai Sahib morning and evening, and Sikh scripture often names God as antarjami, the inner knower of every heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kartaar, the Creator, and your line, spread and gathered. Today, a line about being known, all the way down.

There's a particular loneliness in being misunderstood. You did something for a good reason, and someone took it the worst way. Or you're carrying a pain nobody can see, so people treat you as if you're fine. Or, harder, you did something wrong, you know it, and nobody can see the mess of reasons and hurt underneath. Plenty of people walk around partly hidden, even from those who love them, sometimes especially from them. Chaupai has a line for that hiddenness, and it goes further than you'd expect.
screen: `THE LONELINESS OF BEING MISUNDERSTOOD.` → `PAIN NOBODY CAN SEE.` → `PARTLY HIDDEN, EVEN FROM LOVED ONES.`

segments.voice: The line is ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat, bhale bure kee peer pachhaanat. Ghat ghat: every vessel, every body, every heart. Ke antar kee jaanat: knows what's inside. Bhale bure: the good and the bad. Kee peer pachhaanat: recognizes the pain of. He knows what's within every heart, and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad alike. The first half is something Sikh scripture says often: God is antarjami, the inner knower, who sees from inside. The second half is the surprise. The pain of the bad. Not just the good person's suffering; the wrongdoer's too. The person who hurt you has a pain underneath it, and in this line, God recognizes that as well. It doesn't excuse anything; the same prayer has just asked for wrongdoers to be stopped. But it refuses to pretend that anyone, good or bad, is only their actions. Peer, the word for pain here, is close to an ordinary Punjabi word for an ache, the kind you'd mention to a doctor. That's how close this knowing is. And the other side: if the One knows every heart, you are known, completely. Your good reasons nobody saw. Your hidden ache. Even the tangle behind what you're ashamed of. For some people that sounds frightening. Chaupai sets it inside a prayer for protection, so it's meant to sound like rest. In the prayer's picture, the one praying has nothing to explain. They're already understood.

377.title: Since I held your feet
377.hook: since I grasped Your feet I look to no one else (Chaupai, savaiya)
377.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya as part of Chaupai Sahib, and it is also included in the evening Rehras; touching the feet of elders and teachers is a common sign of deep respect in Punjabi culture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, antarjami, the inner knower, and your line, he knows the pain. Today Chaupai changes shape, near its end.

A busy market, or a big family wedding, and a toddler in the middle of it, holding a parent's leg. Fine, as long as they're holding on. They'll peer out at the noise and the strangers, even smile. The second they let go and lose sight of that leg, the whole world becomes terrifying. The crowd didn't change. What changed was whether they were holding on. Near the end of Chaupai, the meter shifts into a savaiya, a longer, rolling line, and the poet describes exactly that.
screen: `A TODDLER HOLDING A PARENT'S LEG.` → `LET GO, AND THE CROWD IS TERRIFYING.` → `WHAT CHANGED WAS THE HOLDING ON.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the verse begins: since I grasped your feet, I have not brought anyone else under my eye. Feet again. Near the start of the prayer, the mind rested at the Lord's feet. Here the poet has grabbed hold. In South Asian custom, touching someone's feet is what you do before a person you deeply honor, a grandparent, a teacher. To grasp them and not let go is the gesture of someone who has decided where they belong. The verse goes on. In paraphrase: Ram and Rahim, the Puranas and the Qur'an speak of many views, and I have not taken one as my own; the Smritis, Shastras and Vedas tell of many mysteries, and I know none of them; by your grace, O sword-bearer, I have not said this, it is all your own telling. Two things are worth hearing carefully. First, readers take this in more than one way. Sikh teachers often hear it as single-pointed trust rather than a ruling on other scriptures, and point out that the Guru Granth Sahib itself holds the words of Hindu and Muslim saints. On that reading, it's about where the poet's own eyes rest: holding the feet, you stop shopping among opinions. Second, the last line: I have not said this; it's all you. The Tenth Guru, poet, leader, founder of the Khalsa, signs the verse by saying it isn't his. One good word for that posture is trust. Not a list of things believed. A grip. Since I held your feet, the crowd has stopped being frightening.

segments.voice: Notice how many things you're half-holding right now: plans, worries, opinions, backup plans for the backup plans. You don't have to drop them; just choose one thing to trust today, fully, the way a child holds a leg in a crowd, whether God, if you pray, a person who has never let you down, or the fact that you've come through hard days before. Hold it firmly in your mind, and if you pray, say Waheguru as you do.
Charan, feet. Chaupai's savaiya: since I grasped your feet, I look to no one else, and what I've said was never mine.
Your line: held at the feet. Trust is a grip. One more line to go.

378.title: Every other door
378.hook: leaving every other door, I have come to Yours; keep my honor (Chaupai, dohra)
378.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this closing dohra as part of Chaupai Sahib and Rehras, and some say it on its own in moments of fear as a short prayer for protection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, charan, and your line, held at the feet. This week: stay at the feet, end the enemy within, carry them across, spread and gathered, he knows the pain, held at the feet. Today, the very last couplet.

Count the doors you've knocked on in your life. The literal ones: job interviews, the landlord, the new neighbor. And the other kind: the friend you hoped would understand, the qualification that would make you enough, the achievement that was going to fix everything. Some opened. Some didn't. Some opened onto rooms that turned out to be empty. Chaupai ends with someone at the end of that list, having tried them all, standing now at one last door.
screen: `ALL THE DOORS YOU'VE KNOCKED ON.` → `SOME OPENED ONTO EMPTY ROOMS.` → `ONE LAST DOOR.`

segments.voice: The closing couplet, a dohra, goes like this in paraphrase: leaving every other door, I have taken hold of your door. You who have taken my arm, keep my honor. Gobind is your servant. Duaar means door. Sagal duaar, every door. Tuhaaro duaar, your door. And there's the picture from day three hundred seventy-one: baanh gahe, the one who has taken my arm. In Punjabi, to take someone's arm is a promise of protection, the kind you don't walk away from. So the couplet says: you made a promise when you took my arm; keep it, keep my honor. Laaj, the word for honor here, is close to dignity and good name. It's a very human thing to ask: don't let me be shamed. Then the signature. Gobind is your servant. Guru Gobind Singh signs the last line of his prayer not as Guru, not as leader of the Khalsa, but as Gobind das, the servant: the same humility as yesterday's I have not said this. Notice the sequence. The prayer began with a hand and ends with an arm, taken. The heart's wish was to stay at the feet; it ends at the door, having left every other. A whole prayer, one movement: a person walking past every other option to the one place they want to be kept. Some Sikhs say this couplet on its own in moments of fear, as if it carried the whole Chaupai in two lines.

segments.voice: If you can, stand in an open doorway at home, right in the frame, and feel the threshold under your feet: one room behind you, another ahead. Think of the doors you've knocked on, the ones that opened and the ones that didn't, and let them go, one by one. If you pray, say Waheguru, standing at this door; if not, notice how it feels to stop knocking and simply stand.
